audits.title: Management of medically assisted withdrawal from alcohol in acute adult mental health and specialist addictions in-patient services: UK clinical audit findings.
audits.setting: 45 NHS mental health trusts: acute adult wards/PICU and specialist addictions units (POMH audit)

cycle1.result: 908 patients on acute adult wards/PICU and 347 on specialist addictions units; addiction specialist oversight in 33 (4%) of acute ward patients

audits.other_findings: Alcohol history, breath alcohol, Wernicke's screening, parenteral thiamine, relapse prevention and onward referral were all documented more often with specialist addictions care.
audits.citation: Sinclair J, Barnes TRE, Lingford-Hughes A, Drummond C, Loubser I, Rendora O, et al.. Management of medically assisted withdrawal from alcohol in acute adult mental health and specialist addictions in-patient services: UK clinical audit findings. BJPsych Open. 2023;9(3):e61. doi:10.1192/bjo.2023.45. PMID: 37038767.

audits.title: Audit on the Adherence to Guidelines for the Management of Alcohol Withdrawal Syndrome in a General Hospital
audits.standard: Health board policy NU16 for alcohol withdrawal syndrome, based on NICE guidelines
audits.setting: Wards of Wrexham Maelor Hospital (general hospital), Betsi Cadwaladr University Health Board

cycle1.result: Complete drinking history in 4%; physical examination 84%; Wernicke's signs documented 20%; CIWA-Ar applied in 44% and scored correctly in 24%; benzodiazepines prescribed 38%; oral thiamine 58%; alcohol liaison opinion 16%.

audits.intervention: Planned training programmes on alcohol withdrawal by the alcohol liaison team
audits.other_findings: Laboratory investigation compliance ranged from 16% (GGT) to 84% (full blood count); 42% received IV Pabrinex two pairs three times a day.
audits.citation: Simiyon M, Connah R, Proffitt R, Downes S, Jarvis J, Baker C. Audit on the Adherence to Guidelines for the Management of Alcohol Withdrawal Syndrome in a General Hospital. BJPsych Open. 2023;9(Suppl 1):S177-S178.

audits.title: Improving Acute Treatment of Alcohol Withdrawal at an Inpatient De-addiction Ward (‘Vimukthi’) at Kerala State, India: Full Cycle of a Clinical Audit
audits.standard: ASAM, NICE and Government of India guidelines: long-acting benzodiazepines with fixed-dose, symptom-triggered or front-loading regimens according to setting and risk
audits.setting: Dedicated 10-bed inpatient de-addiction ward ('Vimukthi') attached to a general hospital, Kerala

cycle1.result: Fixed-dose regimen of short-acting lorazepam used for all patients; no documentation of risk profiling.

audits.intervention: Standard operating procedure with risk profiling, symptom-triggered regimen using nurse-administered CIWA-Ar and front-loading for high risk, introduced after team discussion and training in October 2023.

cycle2.result: Risk stratification documented (34% low, 52% intermediate, 14% high risk); symptom-triggered regimen given to all patients with front-loading for all high-risk patients; oral lorazepam fell from 3324 mg for 63 patients (Oct–Dec 2022) to 10 mg for 39 patients.

audits.other_findings: Injectable lorazepam use rose by 25% (0.8 mg to 1 mg per patient) and oral diazepam rose from nil to 170 mg. Staff and patients reported satisfaction with the new protocol.
audits.citation: S A, Kuriakose A, Sathiaseelan R. Improving Acute Treatment of Alcohol Withdrawal at an Inpatient De-addiction Ward (‘Vimukthi’) at Kerala State, India: Full Cycle of a Clinical Audit. BJPsych Open. 2024;10(S1):S14-S15. doi:10.1192/bjo.2024.100.

audits.standard: NICE guidelines and Trust policy: physical examination on admission and cognitive assessment before discharge
audits.setting: Bridge House inpatient alcohol detoxification unit

cycle1.result: Physical examination done in 98%; cognitive assessment before discharge in 7%.

audits.other_findings: About 30% had cognitive assessment in the admission plan but it was not actioned before discharge; mean stay about 14 days.

audits.title: A Quality Improvement (QI) Project to Improve Adherence to Alcohol Dependence Guidelines in an Acute Adult Inpatient Setting
audits.standard: Trust Alcohol Dependence Guidelines for assessment and management of alcohol withdrawal
audits.setting: Cedar ward, acute adult psychiatric inpatient unit, Nottinghamshire Healthcare NHS Foundation Trust

cycle1.result: SADQ/weekly alcohol intake documented in 44.4%; regular chlordiazepoxide prescribed per guideline in 55.6% (lower for as-required); escalation for clinical review documented in 25%; CIWA-Ar completed in 23.97%.

audits.intervention: Teaching for nursing staff and resident doctors, alcohol-withdrawal guidance in nursing induction, electronic prescribing prompts for CIWA-Ar, CIWA-Ar and SADQ tools in the electronic record, and guideline review with the Area Prescribing Committee, via PDSA cycles.

cycle2.result: Authors report improved clinician confidence, recognition and documentation of withdrawal symptoms; no figures given.

audits.other_findings: A resident doctor survey found gaps in awareness and process problems on the ward.
audits.citation: Tum A, Senanayake S, Arikan A, Krishnan D, Rajendram M. A Quality Improvement (QI) Project to Improve Adherence to Alcohol Dependence Guidelines in an Acute Adult Inpatient Setting. BJPsych Open. 2026;12(S1):S210-S210. doi:10.1192/bjo.2026.11504.

audits.title: A Re-Audit of the Assessment and Management of Alcohol Misuse Following Admission to the General Adult Inpatient Wards in Mersey Care NHS Foundation Trust
audits.standard: Trust alcohol detoxification policy and NICE guidance
audits.setting: Eight general adult psychiatric inpatient wards, Mersey Care NHS Foundation Trust

cycle1.result: CIWA score documented within 24 hours in 1% of patients with alcohol misuse.

cycle2.result: Alcohol history documented on admission in 55%; weekly intake recorded in 28% of those with prior misuse; CIWA within 24 hours 17%; chlordiazepoxide started in 14%, thiamine 25%, Vitamin B Compound Strong 3%; gamma GT 31%, Mg2+ 25%; 0% offered referral to community alcohol services.

audits.other_findings: A 2022 re-audit showed CIWA within 24 hours in 4%. Referral to community alcohol services worsened compared with earlier audits; clerking proformas and targeted education were recommended.
audits.citation: Wilson J, Rigby E, Hyland D. A Re-Audit of the Assessment and Management of Alcohol Misuse Following Admission to the General Adult Inpatient Wards in Mersey Care NHS Foundation Trust. BJPsych Open. 2026;12(S1):S302-S303. doi:10.1192/bjo.2026.11699.

audits.title: Initial Assessment of Alcohol-Related Psychiatric Admissions: A Clinical Audit From Malta
audits.standard: American Society of Addiction Medicine Clinical Practice Guideline for Alcohol Withdrawal Management
audits.setting: Acute psychiatric inpatient service, Mount Carmel Hospital

cycle1.result: Alcohol use documented in 132 (70%); of 36 regular drinkers, duration of dependency and time of last drink documented in 8.3%, CIWA-A in 66.7%, previous withdrawal delirium, seizures and autonomic activation 0%; urine toxicology 63.9%, LFTs 52.8%, INR 27.8%, ethanol 36.11%.

audits.intervention: Recommended a locally adapted alcohol assessment guideline and re-audit.
audits.other_findings: Comorbidities (100%), other substance use (100%) and suicide risk (91.7%) were well documented.
audits.citation: Pace E, Scicluna S, Camilleri E. Initial Assessment of Alcohol-Related Psychiatric Admissions: A Clinical Audit From Malta. BJPsych Open. 2026;12(S1):S293-S293. doi:10.1192/bjo.2026.11720.

audits.title: An audit of symptom triggered chlordiazepoxide treatment of alcohol withdrawal on a medical admissions unit.
audits.setting: Medical admissions unit, General Infirmary, Leeds

cycle1.result: Patients discharged before resolution of withdrawal symptoms.

audits.title: Evaluation of clinical practice improvement programs for nurses for the management of alcohol withdrawal in hospitals.
audits.standard: Nine clinical standards derived from CIWA-Ar and NSW drug and alcohol withdrawal clinical practice guidelines
audits.setting: Eleven hospitals in an Australian rural area health service; medical records audit

cycle1.result: Baseline compliance with the nine standards measured (figures not given).

audits.intervention: Nurse education: self-directed competency training package (70 nurses, 3 hospitals) or traditional in-service programme (238 nurses, 8 hospitals).

cycle2.result: Hospitals using self-directed competency training had higher total compliance score across the nine standards than in-service hospitals (figures not given).

audits.other_findings: Self-directed competency programme was rated highly by nurses.
audits.citation: Daly M, Kermode S, Reilly D. Evaluation of clinical practice improvement programs for nurses for the management of alcohol withdrawal in hospitals. Contemp Nurse. 2009;31(2):98-107. doi:10.5172/conu.673.31.2.98. PMID: 19379112.

audits.title: Alcohol detoxification in Ysbyty Gwynedd: Two small sips or one big gulp? Two-step screening more reliable for identification of alcohol dependency syndrome at risk of delirium tremens for routine care.
audits.standard: Local pathway for recognition and treatment of alcohol dependency

cycle1.result: Over-prescription of chlordiazepoxide with average length of stay 5.5 days (2012/2013); compliance with screening tools in random samples over three months was persistently low (exact figure unclear in abstract).

audits.intervention: Redesigned pathway with an abbreviated two-question AUDIT screening tool and threshold, implemented over several PDSA cycles.

cycle2.result: 86 patients screened with the two-question tool, 18 at possible risk, 16 had full AUDIT and 8 started detoxification; overall pathway compliance 84%.

audits.other_findings: Common tools (CIWA, AUDIT) were rejected by junior doctors as too cumbersome; the two-question tool had an AUROC of 1.
audits.citation: Salman M, Subbe C. Alcohol detoxification in Ysbyty Gwynedd: Two small sips or one big gulp? Two-step screening more reliable for identification of alcohol dependency syndrome at risk of delirium tremens for routine care. BMJ Qual Improv Rep. 2015;4(1):u206149.w2528. doi:10.1136/bmjquality.u206149.w2528. PMID: 26734413.

audits.title: Alcohol Withdrawal Syndrome: Improving Recognition and Treatment in the Emergency Department.
audits.standard: Use of AUDIT-C screening and CIWA-ar in the emergency department
audits.setting: Emergency department, Southwest Veterans Affairs tertiary care referral centre (Raymond G. Murphy VA Medical Center)

cycle1.result: 12%-15% of patients required escalation of care.

audits.intervention: Education sessions for 35 ED staff led by an advanced practice nurse on AUDIT-C and CIWA-ar.

cycle2.result: No significant difference in use of AUDIT-C or CIWA-ar in the ED and no significant fall in length of stay.

audits.other_findings: Barriers included inability to embed AUDIT-C in the electronic record and inconsistent completion.
audits.citation: Glann JK, Carman M, Thompson J, Olson D, Nuttall C, Fleming H, et al.. Alcohol Withdrawal Syndrome: Improving Recognition and Treatment in the Emergency Department. Adv Emerg Nurs J. 2019;41(1):65-75. doi:10.1097/tme.0000000000000226. PMID: 30702536.

audits.title: Quality Improvement Within a Mental Health Setting: Alcohol Detoxification.
audits.standard: NICE guidelines on alcohol detoxification (history, physical examination including Wernicke's screening, vital signs, liver tests, breath alcohol, standardised withdrawal assessment, chlordiazepoxide and thiamine prescribing); POMH-UK audit
audits.setting: Mental health service, St Patrick's Mental Health Services, Dublin

cycle1.result: First cycle as part of POMH-UK audit showed greater compliance than other services; breath alcohol level documented in 79% and CIWA in 39% (before final cycle).

audits.intervention: Electronic patient records; third cycle focused on breath alcohol level and CIWA documentation.

cycle2.result: Breath alcohol level documentation improved from 79% to 85% and CIWA from 39% to 91% in the final (third) audit cycle.

audits.other_findings: Three cycles in total; the second cycle showed increased compliance in most areas compared with the first.
audits.citation: Doody E, Malone A, Gallagher B, Hopkins K, Weir D, Nolan M, et al.. Quality Improvement Within a Mental Health Setting: Alcohol Detoxification. Ir Med J. 2022;115(1):516. PMID: 35279050.

audits.title: Demonstration of the Managing for Daily Improvement Quality Improvement Methodology in an Alcohol Withdrawal Protocol Audit.
audits.standard: Nurse-driven CIWA-Ar protocol: monitoring frequency, medication administration and medication coverage
audits.setting: 218-bed community hospital, all units (TriStar Summit Medical Center)

cycle1.result: 41 audits collected for 21 patients; compliance figures not reported; most common barrier was lack of communication at shift handoff.

audits.other_findings: Improvement opportunities identified were wider nursing education, protocol auto-discontinuation criteria based on scores, and downtime processes.
audits.citation: Stephens A, Hoot D, Cain A. Demonstration of the Managing for Daily Improvement Quality Improvement Methodology in an Alcohol Withdrawal Protocol Audit. HCA Healthc J Med. 2023;4(2):187-191. doi:10.36518/2689-0216.1617. PMID: 37424968.

audits.title: An audit of the pharmacological management of patients experiencing acute alcohol withdrawal at a large tertiary centre
audits.standard: Local and NICE CG100 guidance: 100% AUDIT-C on admission; 100% CIWA-Ar 4-hourly on day one; 100% benzodiazepine reducing regimen; 100% discharged on thiamine 200-300mg daily where indicated
audits.setting: Acute medical unit, University College London Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust

cycle1.result: AUDIT-C completed 2% (n=1); CIWA-Ar 4-hourly 14% (n=6); correct reducing regimen 23% (n=10); thiamine on discharge 34% (n=15). No standards met.

audits.other_findings: 23% had no benzodiazepine and 30% only PRN; 27% discharged without thiamine.
audits.citation: Hampton E, Saggu R, Gondongwe X, Mamdani F. An audit of the pharmacological management of patients experiencing acute alcohol withdrawal at a large tertiary centre. International Journal of Pharmacy Practice. 2022;30(Supplement_2):ii23-ii23. doi:10.1093/ijpp/riac089.026.
